definition: A Blue Brain electrical type: the neuron fires continuously during a step of current, slowing down as it adapts. Typical of pyramidal cells.
The operation $a = a + w \times x$, the core step of neural-network computation.
Interest earned on earlier interest as well as on the original sum, so growth accelerates over time: FV = PV(1 + r)^n.
Interest paid only on the original sum, never on interest already earned.
What a sum invested today grows to after a number of periods at a given rate.
What a future payment is worth today, found by discounting it at the rate you could earn elsewhere: PV = CF / (1 + r)^n.
The rate used to turn future cash into present value; it reflects the return available on investments of similar risk.
The present value of an investment's future cash flows minus its cost today; positive means it earns more than the discount rate.
The discount rate that makes an investment's net present value zero; for a bond it is the yield to maturity.
A series of equal payments at regular intervals, such as loan payments or bond coupons; also an insurance product that pays income for life or a set term.
A stream of payments that lasts forever, worth C / r, or C1 / (r − g) if it grows at rate g.
The rate actually earned in a year once compounding within the year is counted: (1 + r/m)^m − 1.
A loan's quoted yearly rate, usually without the effect of compounding within the year.
A shortcut: money doubles in about 72 / r years at r percent a year.
Paying off a loan through regular payments that cover interest and part of the principal; also the gradual writing-down of an intangible asset in accounts.
Return after inflation: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1, about nominal minus inflation.
Return in money terms, before adjusting for inflation.
The link between nominal and real rates: 1 + nominal = (1 + real)(1 + inflation).
The constant yearly rate that would turn a starting value into an ending value over the period; the geometric average of returns.
The gap between average and compound returns caused by volatility, roughly σ²/2 a year.
Price change plus income (dividends or interest), as a share of the starting price.
A return that chains sub-period returns and ignores the size and timing of deposits and withdrawals; how funds report performance.
The internal rate of return on an investor's actual cash flows, which reflects when money was added or taken out.
Where new securities are sold by their issuer to investors, as in an IPO or a bond auction.
Where investors trade existing securities with each other, as on a stock exchange.
A company's first sale of shares to the public, after which they trade on an exchange.
The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay (bid) and the lowest a seller will take (ask); a cost of trading.
A dealer who continuously quotes prices to buy and sell a security, earning the spread.
Trading directly between dealers and clients rather than through a central exchange; most bonds, currencies and swaps trade this way.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price.
An order to buy at no more than, or sell at no less than, a set price.
An order that becomes a market order once the price reaches a trigger level; it may fill well below the trigger in a fast market.
The exchange of cash for securities after a trade; one business day after the trade for US stocks since 2024.
A brokerage account that lets you borrow against your holdings to buy more, magnifying gains and losses.
A demand to add cash or securities when losses push equity below the required minimum; if unmet the position is sold.
Selling borrowed shares in the hope of buying them back cheaper; the possible loss is unlimited.
A rapid price rise forced by short sellers buying back to limit their losses.
Share price times shares outstanding: the market value of a company's equity.
The shares available for public trading, excluding large holdings by insiders and governments; most indexes weight by it.
An index of about 500 large US companies weighted by market value; the usual benchmark for US stocks.
A price-weighted index of 30 large US companies, first published in 1896.
Global stock indexes from MSCI: World covers developed markets; ACWI (All Country World Index) adds emerging markets.
A US tax-advantaged retirement account: traditional IRAs give a deduction now and tax withdrawals; Roth IRAs tax contributions and make qualified withdrawals tax-free.
A US employer retirement plan funded from pay before (or, for Roth 401(k)s, after) tax, often with an employer match.
A UK account in which savings and investments grow free of income and capital gains tax, up to a yearly allowance.
Money an employer adds to a retirement plan in proportion to the employee's contributions.
Cash set aside for unexpected expenses, typically three to six months of spending, so investments need not be sold at a bad time.
A cash payment from a company's profits to its shareholders.
A year's dividends divided by the share price.
The first day a stock trades without the right to its next dividend; the price usually drops by about the dividend.
Dividends as a share of earnings.
A company buying its own shares, returning cash to sellers and raising remaining owners' share of the company.
Dividing each share into several, lowering the price per share without changing the company's value.
Shares that pay a fixed dividend ahead of common dividends and rank above common stock in bankruptcy, usually without votes.
Ordinary ownership shares, with votes and a residual claim on profits after everyone else is paid.
A certificate traded in the US that represents shares of a foreign company.
A fall in existing owners' share of a company when new shares are issued.
Size groups by market value: large-cap roughly above \$10 billion, mid-cap \$2 to 10 billion, small-cap \$300 million to \$2 billion.
A stock expected to grow earnings quickly, usually priced at a high multiple of current earnings.
A stock priced cheaply relative to its earnings, book value or cash flow.
A stock whose profits rise and fall with the economy; defensive stocks sell necessities and hold up better in downturns.
The system that sorts listed companies into 11 sectors and finer industry groups.
The annual report a US public company files with the SEC; the 10-Q is its quarterly counterpart.
The SEC's free online database of US company filings.
The US accounting rules; non-GAAP figures are company-adjusted measures that exclude some items.
The accounting rules used by listed companies in most countries outside the US.
The statement of revenue, costs and profit over a period.
A snapshot of what a company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities), with shareholders' equity as the difference.
The statement that reconciles profit to the actual change in cash, split into operating, investing and financing flows.
The money a company takes in from selling goods and services, before costs.
Revenue minus the cost of goods sold, as a share of revenue.
Operating income (EBIT) as a share of revenue.
Profit after all expenses, interest and taxes.
Earnings before interest and taxes: profit from operations regardless of how the company is financed.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; a rough measure of operating cash generation that ignores the cost of replacing assets.
Net income divided by shares outstanding.
Spreading the cost of equipment and buildings over their useful lives as an expense.
The premium paid for an acquisition above the fair value of its identifiable assets, carried on the balance sheet.
Assets minus liabilities as recorded in the accounts; what owners would get if everything sold at book values.
Current assets minus current liabilities; changes in it make cash flow differ from profit.
Money spent on long-term assets such as equipment and buildings.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: cash the business produces beyond what it needs to sustain and grow itself.
Net income divided by shareholders' equity.
After-tax operating profit divided by the capital invested in the business (debt plus equity minus cash).
Splitting ROE into net margin × asset turnover × leverage to see where it comes from.
EBIT divided by interest expense: how easily a company pays its interest.
Debt minus cash; often compared with EBITDA to gauge leverage.
The part of earnings not yet received or paid in cash; high accruals have predicted weaker future returns.
Share price divided by earnings per share: what investors pay for a dollar of yearly profit.
Earnings per share divided by price, the inverse of the P/E.
The P/E divided by the expected earnings growth rate in percent.
Market capitalization divided by book value.
Market capitalization plus debt minus cash (and other claims): the value of the whole business, used in EV/EBITDA comparisons.
Price divided by the average of ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings; high values have preceded lower long-run returns.
Value = next year's dividend / (required return − growth), for dividends growing at a constant rate forever.
Valuing a business as the present value of its expected future free cash flows plus a terminal value.
In a DCF, the value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast years, usually by the Gordon formula.
The blended required return on a company's debt (after tax) and equity, used to discount its free cash flows.
The return shareholders require, often estimated with CAPM.
Solving for the growth that today's price implies, instead of computing a value from a forecast.
Buying well below estimated value so that errors in the estimate don't cause a loss.
A durable competitive advantage that protects a company's profits from rivals.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest (coupons) and returns the principal at maturity.
The amount a bond repays at maturity, usually 100 per 100 or \$1,000.
A bond's yearly interest payment as a percentage of face value.
The date a bond's principal is repaid.
A bond that pays no coupons and is sold below face value; its return is the rise to par.
A bond the issuer may repay early, usually when rates have fallen.
The single discount rate that makes a bond's cash flows equal its price; its return if held to maturity with coupons reinvested at that rate.
A bond's yearly coupon divided by its price.
The lowest yield a bond can give across every date the issuer could repay it.
Coupon interest earned since the last payment, paid by a bond's buyer on top of the quoted clean price.
A bond's price sensitivity to yields: price falls about D% for each 1-point rise in yield. Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to its cash flows.
The curvature of a bond's price-yield relation; positive convexity means gains from falling yields exceed losses from equal rises.
The change in a bond's value for a one-basis-point (0.01%) change in yield.
One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%).
A set of bonds maturing in successive years, giving regular repayments and smoothing interest-rate risk.
The risk that coupons and maturing bonds must be reinvested at lower rates.
US government zero-coupon debt maturing within a year; the usual measure of the risk-free rate.
US government coupon debt: notes mature in 2 to 10 years, bonds in 20 or 30.
US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, giving a known real yield.
US savings bonds sold to individuals, paying a fixed rate plus an inflation rate; they cannot lose value.
The nominal Treasury yield minus the TIPS yield of the same maturity: the inflation rate at which both return the same.
UK government bonds.
German federal government bonds, the benchmark for the euro area.
Bonds issued by the Japanese government.
A bond issued by a US state, city or local agency; interest is usually exempt from federal income tax.
The taxable yield that would match a tax-free yield after tax: tax-free yield / (1 − tax rate).
A bond backed by a pool of home loans, whose payments pass through to investors.
Bonds issued by a national government.
A rating agency's grade of a borrower's ability to pay, from AAA down to D.
Bonds rated BBB−/Baa3 or higher.
A bond rated below investment grade, paying a higher yield for its higher default risk.
A bond cut from investment grade to high yield.
The extra yield a bond pays over a government bond of the same maturity.
Failure to make a promised payment of interest or principal.
The share of a defaulted debt's face value that creditors eventually get back.
The chance that a borrower defaults within a period, often a year.
The mix and ranking of a company's debt and equity, which decides who is paid first in a failure.
In bankruptcy, each class of claim is paid in full before any lower class gets anything.
Debt that ranks ahead of other (subordinated or junior) debt for repayment.
A promise in a loan or bond agreement that restricts what the borrower may do.
A bond that can be exchanged for a set number of the issuer's shares.
A contract in which one side pays a yearly premium and the other pays the loss if a named borrower defaults.
In Merton's model, how many standard deviations a firm's asset value is above its debt; it drives the estimated default probability.
The institution that issues a currency, sets its short-term interest rates and acts as lender of last resort.
The US central bank.
The overnight rate at which US banks lend reserves to each other, targeted by the Federal Reserve.
The Federal Reserve committee that sets US monetary policy.
The central bank for the euro area.
Japan's central bank.
The UK's central bank.
The US overnight rate on Treasury repo trades, which replaced LIBOR as the benchmark for dollar loans and derivatives.
Central bank purchases of long-term bonds with new reserves to push down long-term rates; quantitative tightening reverses it.
A central bank's statements about the likely path of future rates.
A formula for the policy rate based on the neutral rate, inflation's gap from target and the output gap.
Government yields plotted against maturity; inverted when short yields exceed long ones.
The extra yield investors demand to hold long bonds rather than roll short ones.
The theory that long yields equal the average of expected future short rates.
A future interest rate implied by today's yields for different maturities.
A measure of the prices of a basket of consumer goods and services; core versions exclude food and energy.
The US price index of personal consumption expenditures, which the Federal Reserve targets.
A rise in the general level of prices, which lowers the buying power of money.
A pooled fund bought and sold at its net asset value once a day.
A fund whose shares trade on an exchange all day like a stock.
A fund that holds the securities of an index in index weights instead of picking.
Picking securities in an attempt to beat a benchmark.
A fund's assets minus liabilities, per share.
A fund's yearly fees as a percentage of assets.
A commission charged when buying or selling some mutual funds.
The share of a fund's holdings replaced in a year; high turnover means higher hidden trading costs.
How much a fund's return deviates from its benchmark's; tracking difference is the average gap.
A fund with a fixed number of shares that trade on an exchange, often at a discount or premium to NAV.
A fund holding very short, high-quality debt, aiming to keep a stable price of \$1.
A fund that shifts from stocks toward bonds as a chosen retirement year approaches.
The planned change in a target-date fund's mix over time.
An ETF that aims for a multiple (or the inverse) of an index's daily return; over longer periods its return can differ greatly from that multiple.
Index strategies that weight by factors such as value, size, momentum or low volatility instead of market value.
Weighting each holding by its market value, as most indexes do.
Sharpe's point that before costs the average active dollar earns the market return, so after costs it must trail the average passive dollar.
S&P's scorecards comparing active funds with their benchmark indexes.
A simple portfolio of a home stock index fund, an international stock index fund and a bond index fund.
The market for trading one currency for another.
Two currencies quoted against each other, as BASE/QUOTE: the price is units of the quote currency per unit of the base.
The usual smallest price step in a currency pair: 0.0001 for most, 0.01 for yen pairs.
An exchange rate between two currencies, neither of which is the US dollar.
The exchange rate for immediate delivery (normally two business days).
A spot currency trade paired with an opposite forward trade, used to fund in another currency.
The most-traded currency pairs against the dollar: EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD and NZD/USD.
A currency held in large amounts by central banks as part of their foreign reserves; above all the US dollar.
A currency that tends to rise in market turmoil, such as the yen, the Swiss franc and the US dollar.
A low-interest-rate currency borrowed to finance carry trades, classically the yen or Swiss franc.
A currency that moves with prices of a country's commodity exports, such as the Australian and Canadian dollars and the Norwegian krone.
A policy fixing a currency's value to another currency or basket, defended by the central bank.
The idea that the dollar strengthens both when the world is in crisis and when the US economy leads, and weakens in between.
Borrowing in a low-interest currency to invest in a higher-interest one, earning the rate gap unless the exchange rate moves against you.
A rush to close carry trades, which sharply lifts funding currencies such as the yen.
The arbitrage link setting a forward exchange rate at spot adjusted by the two currencies' interest rates.
The theory that higher-yielding currencies should depreciate by the rate gap; it fails over short horizons, which is the forward premium puzzle.
The idea that exchange rates adjust so goods cost the same everywhere; relative PPP says currencies move by inflation differences over time.
An exchange rate adjusted for relative price levels; the effective version uses a trade-weighted basket.
Removing currency risk from a foreign investment, usually by selling the foreign currency forward.
The difference between the forward and spot exchange rates, set by the interest-rate gap.
A property's net operating income divided by its value.
A property's rental income minus operating costs, before financing.
A company that owns income-producing property and pays out most of its income as dividends.
Raw materials such as oil, metals and crops, traded in standardized forms.
When later futures prices are above nearer ones; rolling long positions then loses money.
When later futures prices are below nearer ones; rolling long positions then earns a positive roll yield.
The gain or loss from replacing an expiring futures contract with a later one.
The benefit of holding a physical commodity rather than a futures contract on it.
Funds that buy whole companies, often with borrowed money, to improve and sell them.
Funds that invest in young, fast-growing private companies.
Loans made directly by investment funds to companies rather than by banks or in bond markets.
A lightly regulated pooled fund that can short, use leverage and trade derivatives, usually with high fees.
The traditional hedge fund fee: 2% of assets a year plus 20% of profits.
Reported values of private assets lagging the market, which understates their volatility and correlation.
Overstating past results by studying only funds, companies or investors that survived.
The first cryptocurrency, launched in 2009, with a fixed maximum supply of 21 million coins.
A crypto token designed to hold a steady value, usually \$1, by holding dollar assets.
A contract whose value depends on the price of something else.
A private agreement to buy or sell an asset on a future date at a price fixed today.
A standardized forward contract traded on an exchange and cleared through a clearinghouse, settled daily.
The exchange-linked body that stands between both sides of every futures trade and guarantees performance.
The deposit required to open a futures or margin position; maintenance margin is the minimum it may fall to before a call.
Valuing a position at current market prices, and in futures settling gains and losses in cash each day.
The financing and storage cost, minus income, of holding an asset; it sets the forward price relative to spot.
The difference between an asset's spot price and its futures price.
The size of a hedging position relative to the exposure being hedged.
A contract exchanging fixed-rate payments for floating-rate payments on a notional amount.
A contract that pays the total return of an asset in exchange for a financing rate.
The reference amount on which a swap's payments are calculated, usually never exchanged.
A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell something at a set price by or on a set date.
The right to buy at the strike price.
The right to sell at the strike price.
The price at which an option may be exercised.
The price paid for an option.
The last date on which an option can be exercised.
American options can be exercised any time before expiry; European options only at expiry.
An option is in the money when exercising it now would pay something; at the money when the price is near the strike; out of the money when exercise would pay nothing.
What an option would pay if exercised now: max(S − K, 0) for a call.
An option's price minus its intrinsic value; it shrinks to zero by expiry.
C + K e^(−rT) = P + S: the arbitrage link between European call and put prices.
The volatility that makes an option-pricing model match an option's market price.
An index of the S&P 500's 30-day implied volatility, often called the fear gauge.
The tendency of implied volatility to exceed the volatility that later occurs, which pays option sellers on average.
A long-dated call option issued by a company on its own shares.
Shares (or options) granted to employees as pay, vesting over time.
Owning shares and selling a call on them: income now in exchange for capping gains above the strike.
Selling a put while holding the cash to buy the shares if assigned.
Owning shares and buying a put, which limits the loss below the strike.
Owning shares, buying a put below and selling a call above, limiting both loss and gain.
Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike, limiting both cost and gain.
A call and a put at the same strike and expiry: long it to profit from a big move either way.
An out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put on the same expiry.
Selling an OTM put and call and buying further-out ones to cap the loss: a bet the price stays in a range.
Buy one low-strike, sell two middle-strike, buy one high-strike option: pays most if the price ends at the middle strike.
Selling a near-dated option and buying a later one at the same strike.
Being required to fulfil a short option's obligation when the holder exercises.
Pricing options on a tree of up and down moves by working back from expiry with risk-neutral probabilities.
Pricing a derivative as its expected payoff discounted at the risk-free rate, using probabilities under which assets grow at that rate.
A mix of the underlying asset and borrowing that copies a derivative's payoff, so it must cost the same.
The 1973 formula for the price of a European option from the stock price, strike, time, interest rate and volatility.
Implied volatility differing by strike; for stock indexes, low-strike puts have higher implied volatility.
Sensitivities of an option's value: delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho.
The change in an option's value per \$1 change in the underlying price; also the hedge ratio.
The rate of change of an option's delta as the underlying moves.
The change in an option's value per day as time passes.
The change in an option's value per one-point change in implied volatility.
The change in an option's value for a change in interest rates.
The standard deviation of returns: the typical size of swings around the average.
A fall from a previous peak; the maximum drawdown is the worst such fall over a period.
Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by volatility.
Excess return divided by downside deviation, which counts only returns below a target.
Active return over a benchmark divided by tracking error.
Return above what an asset's risk exposures (such as beta) would predict.
An asset's sensitivity to the market: cov(asset, market) / var(market).
A measure from −1 to +1 of how two returns move together.
Extreme outcomes occurring more often than a normal distribution predicts.
A rare, extreme, hard-to-predict event with large consequences.
A loss level that should be exceeded only with a small probability over a set period.
The average loss in the worst cases beyond the value-at-risk level.
The return on an investment with no default risk, usually short-term government bills.
The extra return expected from stocks over risk-free assets.
Spreading money across assets that don't move together, lowering risk without lowering expected return proportionally.
Risk peculiar to one company or asset, which diversification removes.
Risk shared across the market that diversification cannot remove.
Markowitz's framework for choosing portfolios by expected return, volatility and correlation.
The set of portfolios with the highest expected return for each level of risk.
The line from the risk-free rate through the maximum-Sharpe (tangency) portfolio: the best mixes of cash and risky assets.
E[R] = rf + β(E[Rm] − rf): expected return rises with market beta only.
CAPM's line of required return against beta.
Factor models explaining stock returns by market, size, value and later profitability and investment.
The historical excess return of small companies over large.
The historical excess return of cheap (high book-to-market) stocks over expensive ones.
The tendency of recent winners to keep outperforming for several months.
Ross's theory that expected returns depend linearly on exposures to several systematic factors.
Profiting risk-free from a price difference between equivalent assets.
The theory that prices reflect available information, so beating the market consistently after costs is very hard.
A portfolio method that starts from market-implied returns and blends in an investor's views.
Weighting assets so each contributes equal risk, usually with leverage on bonds.
The split of a portfolio between asset classes such as stocks, bonds and cash.
A group of investments with similar characteristics, such as stocks, bonds, cash, real estate or commodities.
A balanced mix of 60% stocks and 40% bonds.
Investors' tendency to overweight their own country's assets.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals rather than all at once.
Investing available money all at once.
Moving in and out of markets based on forecasts; it has a poor record.
Trading to bring a portfolio back to its target mix.
Choosing which accounts hold which assets to reduce taxes.
Bengen's finding that withdrawing 4% of the starting balance, raised yearly with inflation, survived 30 years in US history.
The danger that poor returns early in withdrawals deplete a portfolio even if later returns are good.
A written plan of goals, allocation, rebalancing rules and behavior in crises.
The US government retirement pension; claiming later raises the monthly benefit.
Kahneman and Tversky's model of decisions under risk: outcomes judged as gains or losses from a reference point, with losses weighted more.
Feeling losses about twice as strongly as equal gains.
The tendency to sell winners too soon and hold losers too long.
Overrating one's own knowledge or skill, which leads to excessive trading.
Following what others are doing, especially buying after big rises.
Expecting recent trends to continue.
Relying too heavily on an initial number, such as the purchase price.
Seeking information that supports existing beliefs.
Treating money differently depending on its source or label.
The costs and risks that stop rational traders from correcting mispricings.
Prices rising far above fundamental value on expectations of further rises, usually ending in a crash.
Testing a strategy on historical data.
Finding patterns by testing many ideas on the same data, many of which are flukes.
Using information in a backtest that was not available at the time.
Testing a rule on data it was not designed on.
A Sharpe ratio adjusted for the number of strategies tried and for non-normal returns.
Kenneth French's free online data of factor and portfolio returns back to 1926.
A framework for industry competition: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power and buyer power.
Profit from selling an asset for more than its cost; taxed at lower rates when held long term in many countries.
US dividends taxed at long-term capital gains rates when holding-period rules are met.
What you paid for an investment, used to compute the taxable gain.
Selling investments at a loss to offset gains, while staying invested through a similar holding.
A US rule disallowing a tax loss if the same or a substantially identical security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale.
The reset of an inherited asset's cost basis to its value at death.
Moving money from a traditional retirement account to a Roth account, paying tax now so later withdrawals are tax-free.
An adviser legally bound to act in the client's best interest.
An automated service that builds and rebalances a portfolio for a low fee.
A fraud paying earlier investors with new investors' money while reporting fictitious returns.
Hyping a thinly traded asset to sell into the buying it creates.
Investment fraud that targets members of a community through trust.
A 3.8% US tax on investment income above certain income levels.
